fig19_1: Two panels. Left: line plot of the mapped coordinate y versus the computational coordinate x over minus pi to pi, with one S-shaped curve per width parameter ell of 0.1, 0.3, 1.0, 3.0, and 10.0; a dashed grey diagonal marks the identity at ell equals one. Curves for ell below one are steep through the origin and flat near the edges; curves for ell above one show the opposite. Right: five stacked horizontal bands, each showing the images of a uniform twenty-four-point x-grid as tick marks for one ell value. The ticks bunch near y equals zero for small ell, near y equals plus or minus pi for large ell, and stay evenly spaced at ell equals one, making the clustering trade-off visible.
fig19_2: Four panels comparing a sharp periodic pulse on a uniform Fourier grid versus an arctan over tan mapped grid. Panel a plots the pulse profile f of y as a solid line with the two thirty-two-point grids overlaid, uniform Fourier as offset crosses and mapped grid as circles clustered near the peak. Panel b shows the same pulse in computational coordinates: the broadened mapped profile in teal is about five times wider and smoother than the original dashed grey pulse, with the uniform x-grid beneath. Panel c plots L-infinity error against N on a semilog axis; the uniform grid reaches machine precision near N of one hundred twenty-eight while the mapped grid reaches it near N of sixty-four. Panel d plots Fourier-coefficient magnitudes at N of ninety-six on a semilog axis, both decaying geometrically but the mapped spectrum falling off markedly faster.
fig19_3: Two panels comparing two arithmetic implementations of the same Chebyshev solver for a boundary-value problem with exact solution sine of pi x. The left panel overlays the computed interpolant at N of twenty-four on the exact solution, the two indistinguishable. The right panel plots max-norm error versus N on a semilog axis for the X-path using a dense differentiation matrix and the T-path using FFT-based cosine differentiation; both curves drop steeply and reach machine precision near N of twenty, differing only by a small constant factor at the floating-point noise floor.
tbl19_1: Table reporting median wall-clock solve times and final max-norm errors for the X-path and T-path at N from thirty-two to five hundred twelve, showing the dense-matrix X-path runs several times faster than the FFT-based T-path across this range while both reach comparable near-machine-precision accuracy.
fig19_4: Four panels demonstrating a reusable one-dimensional map toolkit. Panel a shows the bounded tanh map y equals tanh of x over the interval minus one to one, with Chebyshev-Gauss-Lobatto nodes as ticks along the bottom and their compressed images as ticks on the right edge, joined by faint dotted elbow guide lines. Panel b shows the algebraic semi-infinite map at ell of two stretching toward infinity, with the y-axis cut off at twelve and several node images lying above the visible range. Panel c plots max-norm error of the first mapped derivative versus N on a semilog axis for both maps, both reaching machine precision near N of fifty. Panel d plots the same for the second derivative, the curves shifted upward by roughly the logarithm of N squared at every N, illustrating the N-squared accuracy lag of differentiating twice.
fig19_5: Four panels comparing domain truncation against an algebraic map for a decaying semi-infinite problem. Panel a overlays the computed solution at N of twenty-four: coral circles for truncation at L of twenty and teal squares for the algebraic map at ell of two, clipped at y of twelve. Panel b plots the algebraic map for ell of one, two, four, and eight, showing how small ell packs points near the origin and large ell stretches them outward, with Chebyshev nodes as ticks along the bottom. Panel c plots truncation error versus N on a semilog axis for three truncation lengths, each plateauing at its e-to-the-minus-L floor. Panel d plots algebraic-map error versus N for four ell values, every curve descending geometrically to machine precision with no accuracy floor; at N of forty-eight the best map reaches about ten to the minus twelve versus about ten to the minus eight for the best truncation.
fig19_6: Four panels on healing a square-root branch-point singularity. Panel a plots the target square root of one minus X squared in physical coordinates against the smooth sech of y in mapped coordinates. Panel b plots pointwise error at N of thirty-two versus the physical coordinate on a semilog axis: the direct expansion is uniformly poor with sharp peaks at the endpoints X equals plus or minus one, while the tanh-mapped expansion stays near machine precision in the interior and rises only gently near the boundaries. Panel c plots max-norm error versus N on a log-log axis, the direct expansion tracking a one-over-N guide line while the tanh-mapped expansion descends geometrically, reaching about ten to the minus nine at N of one hundred twenty-eight. Panel d plots Chebyshev coefficient magnitudes at N of sixty-four, the direct expansion showing an algebraic one-over-n-squared envelope and the mapped expansion a steep geometric decay.
fig19_7: A two-by-three layout for a square Poisson problem with corner stress. Top row: panel a is a contour plot of the solution at N of thirty-two, with roughly circular level sets and mild flattening toward the corners; panel b shows the one-dimensional physical grids at N of twenty-four, the standard Chebyshev grid and the tanh-clustered grid with alpha of two agreeing in the interior but differing sharply near the endpoints; panel c plots max-norm error against the reference versus N on a semilog axis for the unmapped method and tanh clustering at alpha of one, two, and three, with the unmapped method winning at every resolution up to N of sixty-four. Bottom row, panels d through f: pointwise error fields at N of twenty-four on a shared logarithmic color scale for the unmapped method, tanh alpha of one, and tanh alpha of three, showing that aggressive clustering pushes error away from the corners and into the interior without lowering the overall norm.
fig19_8: Four panels sweeping the width parameter of the arctan over tan map for a localized periodic pulse. Panel a shows three mapped thirty-two-point grids for ell of 0.1, 0.3, and 1.0 with the pulse profile drawn for reference, smaller ell clustering points near the pulse at y equals zero. Panel b shows the pulse in computational coordinates at the chosen ell of 0.3, the broadened teal profile about five times wider than the original dashed grey pulse with the uniform x-grid beneath. Panel c is a filled error landscape over N and ell, revealing a broad dark valley of good parameter choices. Panel d plots error versus ell at several fixed N on a semilog axis, the optimum drifting from about 0.15 at N of sixteen to about 0.45 at N of sixty-four with valleys decades wide, showing low sensitivity to fine tuning.
fig19_9: Four panels on the Kosloff-Tal-Ezer map trade-off between accuracy and timestep. Panel a plots the map for three regimes: standard Chebyshev as the straight identity, aggressive beta near one over N squared which is nearly straight, and conservative beta retaining a clear S-shape, with input nodes as ticks along the bottom. Panel b plots minimum grid spacing versus N on a log-log axis, standard scaling like one over N squared and aggressive like the gentler one over N. Panel c plots the spectral radius of the first-derivative matrix versus N, aggressive KTE cutting stiffness by nearly an order of magnitude at N of ninety-six. Panel d plots the Chebyshev coefficient magnitude of f equals y versus N on a log-log axis with a theoretical 0.488 over N squared asymptote; aggressive KTE follows this algebraic decay, destroying geometric convergence, while conservative KTE drops to the floating-point floor and preserves it.
